Use the substitution

\[
x=\cos\theta,\qquad 0\le \theta\le \frac{\pi}{2}.
\]

This is one-to-one on \([0,1]\). First check endpoints:

- If \(x=0\), the left-hand side is \(0\neq 1\).
- If \(x=1\), the left-hand side is \(8(1)(-1)(1)=-8\neq 1\).

So any root in \([0,1]\) corresponds to some \(\theta\in(0,\pi/2)\).

Now

\[
1-2x^2=1-2\cos^2\theta=-\cos 2\theta,
\]

and

\[
8x^4-8x^2+1=8\cos^4\theta-8\cos^2\theta+1=\cos 4\theta.
\]

Thus the left-hand side becomes

\[
8\cos\theta(-\cos 2\theta)(\cos 4\theta)
=-8\cos\theta\cos 2\theta\cos 4\theta.
\]

Using

\[
\sin 8\theta=8\sin\theta\cos\theta\cos 2\theta\cos 4\theta,
\]

we get

\[
-8\cos\theta\cos 2\theta\cos 4\theta
=-\frac{\sin 8\theta}{\sin\theta}.
\]

Therefore the equation becomes

\[
-\frac{\sin 8\theta}{\sin\theta}=1,
\]

or equivalently, since \(\sin\theta>0\) on \((0,\pi/2)\),

\[
\sin 8\theta+\sin\theta=0.
\]

Using sum-to-product,

\[
\sin 8\theta+\sin\theta
=2\sin\frac{9\theta}{2}\cos\frac{7\theta}{2}.
\]

So we need

\[
2\sin\frac{9\theta}{2}\cos\frac{7\theta}{2}=0.
\]

For \(0<\theta<\pi/2\):

1. \(\sin\frac{9\theta}{2}=0\)

\[
\frac{9\theta}{2}=n\pi
\implies
\theta=\frac{2n\pi}{9}.
\]

Since \(0<\theta<\pi/2\), we get \(n=1,2\), giving

\[
\theta=\frac{2\pi}{9},\quad \frac{4\pi}{9}.
\]

2. \(\cos\frac{7\theta}{2}=0\)

\[
\frac{7\theta}{2}=\frac{\pi}{2}+n\pi
\implies
\theta=\frac{(2n+1)\pi}{7}.
\]

Since \(0<\theta<\pi/2\), we get \(n=0,1\), giving

\[
\theta=\frac{\pi}{7},\quad \frac{3\pi}{7}.
\]

Thus there are four distinct values of \(\theta\), and since \(x=\cos\theta\) is one-to-one on \([0,\pi/2]\), they give four distinct roots in \([0,1]\).

\[
\boxed{4}
\]
